role: The second reading: each entry read to refute it, not to admire it.
method: Each fragment read whole beside what show.cjs prints for the grape (GRAPES, GRAPES_PLUS, TASTE, INTRO_GRAPES, GRID_SAY, GRID_READS, the service rows) and beside the Codex's region records, banks and service reference where they name the grape or a place the entry leans on.

Every fact the Codex's reviewed records do not already state was put to search, at most five searches a grape: the first records, the parentage, the synonyms, the appellation rules, the places under abroad, and the notes of the glass where the author marked one as unsourced.

The glass read as a blind taster would: each note asked whether a taster would nod, each prose field scanned for a family word in disguise, and each ladder set beside the Court's grid read and beside the other five entries of the chunk.

The four lines counted and said aloud for the five beats in order; the sale read for its two sentences; the cards and questions read for one key, four options of one kind, no option shut out by the stem and no key that stands out by its form; the compare tells read from both sides against every fragment that names these grapes.
node .scripts/grapes/build-grapes.cjs --lint --chunk g2 run after every round of edits until it printed six of six sound. The writing build was never run and no other file was touched.

A last pass read the six again after the first two rounds were pushed: every prose field scanned once more for a family word dressed as an adjective, each cause in a why line read against the cellar line of the same entry, and three more searches made (one for Silvaner, two for Müller-Thurgau) on what the first rounds left unsettled.
limits: This session reached search alone: no source address could be opened. The hosts www.winesofgermany.com, www.altoadigewines.com and www.nzwine.com did not resolve from here, and the Alsace body was not tried again. A page is cited as search results quoted it.
Where an address names a producer it is left out and the source is cited by its title alone.
The lint's three notes on the word spice in the Gewürztraminer entry were read and left: each gives the meaning of the word Gewürz.

The first record: a cellar account of 13 March 1435 at Rüsselsheim, for vines bought for a count of Katzenelnbogen. Confirmed in two sources; the count stays unnamed.

The ladder against the Court's grid and the Codex's region records: the Mosel and Rheingau cool, as the grid reads them; the Pfalz a warm, dry strip; the Clare Valley hot days and cold nights. Alsace is cool in the Court's read and was on the moderate rung.
worlds: the call put to a flight that holds a dry Alsace, a Wachau and a dry German wine; the why read for its causes; the two cellar lines read against the two glass lines of the same entry.
Service against the Codex's rows (light aromatic whites at 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, a white wine glass, decanting usually unnecessary, the crystals) and TASTE.age: agree.
The labels (trocken, feinherb, the three grades, Grosses Gewächs), the petrol answer and the three questions for one key each.
Compare tells from both sides with Chenin Blanc, Grüner Veltliner, Sémillon, Silvaner and Müller-Thurgau: agree.

changed.was: Sweetness, low alcohol and wet slate lean Mosel; bone dry lime juice at moderate alcohol, with early toast or petrol, leans Clare or Eden Valley.
changed.now: Sweetness at low alcohol, or peach on a fuller dry frame, leans Old World; taut, bone dry lime with early toast or petrol leans Australia.
changed.why: The call would not survive a flight. It parted the Mosel from the Clare Valley and sent every dry Alsace, Wachau and German wine, bone dry at moderate alcohol, to Australia. The entry's own Old World glass says those wines are usually dry and fuller, and its moderate rung gives them ripe peach and apricot. The second card and the worlds question keep the Mosel against the Clare Valley, the pair they name.

changed.now: so acidity stays high and a little sweetness is kept to balance it
changed.why: Sugar low and sweetness kept read as a contradiction in one clause. The Court's grid read gives the cause plainly: high acidity and tart, just ripe fruit near the northern limit for ripening.

changed.was: Usually fermented cold in steel until fully dry, kept away from oak and air, and bottled early under screwcap to hold the freshness.
changed.now: Usually fermented cold in steel, kept away from oak and air, and bottled early under screwcap; Australia ferments it fully dry.
changed.why: The New World glass of the same entry says the Finger Lakes and Washington range from dry to sweet, so fully dry belongs to Australia alone.

changed.was: a slaty edge

changed.why: The second card keeps wet slate as the Mosel's mark. Slate on both sides of one contrast teaches nothing. (Polish Hill River does lie on slate, and its wines are called flintier.)

codexRecords: js/data-grid.js, the Gewürztraminer read: Alsace is cool. Three ladders of this chunk now agree with it; the Riesling and Muscat Blanc ladders had Alsace as moderate.

js/data-intro.js, the Régionale rows: Gewürztraminer's aroma line says baking spice and Silvaner's says earthy, herbal. The author's flags, confirmed: family words. The rows are the Régionale course's own and are left alone; the table names the things.
js/reference.js, Grüner Veltliner's other line: green herbs, a family word. The Riesling tell that had copied it now says celery.
js/data-tasting.js, TASTE.age for Riesling: ages further than any other white. The entry says almost any other, the safer claim.

js/data-tasting.js, TASTE.world reads old for Riesling, Gewürztraminer and Muscat Blanc while the plan fixes contrast. No fault in either: the flag says where the grape is from, the plan what a guest meets on a list.

js/data-regions.js, the Rutherglen ladder's indicative ages (about 3 to 5, 6 to 10, 11 to 19, 20 and more years): the author's doubt. One trade source repeats those figures and the growers' own material says age is one factor among several. The record is hedged and stands.
js/data-service-ref.js, the faults: geranium taint. No fault in the record; it is why geranium left the Müller-Thurgau glass.
unsettled: Whether every source address still answers: none could be opened from this session.

Whether the Alto Adige consortium names lilac for Müller-Thurgau (it may be the elderflower under its other German name), and five to ten grams of sugar a litre for Gewürztraminer: both are the author's readings.
Whether Müller-Thurgau is grown in every German region: the entry now says across the country.
Muscat Blanc's mode: contrast as the plan fixes it, though the difference is of method as much as of world.
Gisborne on the moderate rung for Gewürztraminer, against the Codex's own word for it, a warm coast.
Quince for Silvaner, and mace and lilac for Müller-Thurgau: tasters' notes with no source read behind them.
Ginger in the spice group for Grüner Veltliner: a note of ripe Smaragd with no source read behind it.
settled: The day of Silvaner's first German record: 6 April 1659 is the planting at Castell, on the German wine body's own page; 5 April is the purchase.
